sermon:
## The Voice Behind You
*Revelation is the unveiling of Christ, who walks among His churches and holds the keys of death*

**Text:** Revelation 1 · **Supporting:** Daniel 7:13-14 · Isaiah 6:1-5 · Hebrews 4:15 · Colossians 1:18

We treat Revelation as a cipher. A puzzle for the clever, a timeline for the anxious, a book about the future that has almost nothing to say about the Tuesday we are actually living. That is the first lie the book corrects. Its opening word is not *future*. Its opening word is *unveiling* — *apokalypsis*, the pulling back of a curtain — and the thing behind the curtain is a Person.

**Not a code. A face.**

John tells us where he was when the curtain moved. "I, John, your brother and partner in the tribulation and the kingdom and the patient endurance that are in Jesus, was on the island called Patmos on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus" (Revelation 1:9). Patmos was not a retreat. It was exile, a penal rock in the Aegean for a man Rome found inconvenient. The whole book is written from inside the cost. Before John sees a single throne, he is a prisoner. The first reader was a suffering church, and the book is pastoral before it is predictive. It exists to keep faith alive when faith is expensive.

Then the voice. "I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet" (Revelation 1:10). Behind him. The risen Christ does not announce Himself from a stage out in front where John can compose his face. He speaks from behind, where you cannot prepare, where you have to turn. And when John turns he does not see a friend. He sees something closer to what Isaiah saw in the temple in the year King Uzziah died, when the prophet cried, "Woe is me. For I am lost" (Isaiah 6:5). John sees one "like a son of man," the very phrase Daniel used for the one who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom that shall not be destroyed (Daniel 7:13-14), and his hair is white, his eyes are fire, his face is the sun at full strength.

And John, the apostle who leaned on Jesus' chest at supper, falls down as though dead.

**He is the same Jesus. He is not the tame one.**

We have made our peace with a manageable Christ. The friend in the corner, the helper on call, the one who exists to make our lives go better. Revelation will not let that stand. The Jesus who walked dusty roads and let a fisherman lean on Him is the Jesus whose voice now sounds like rushing waters and whose word comes out of His mouth like a sword. We did not lose the intimacy. We forgot the glory underneath it. And a church that forgets the glory will eventually stop fearing anything but the world.

I have done this. I have preached a Jesus small enough to fit my sermon and never large enough to frighten me into obedience. A Christ I could use is a Christ I will not worship, and a church full of pastors using Him is exactly the church that lies down in front of the empire and calls it wisdom.

But look at what His hand does. John lies there like a corpse, and "he laid his right hand on me, saying, Fear not" (Revelation 1:17). The hand that holds seven stars reaches down to the man it just leveled. This is the whole gospel in one gesture. The glory that undoes you is the mercy that lifts you. We have a high priest who is not unable to sympathize with our weakness (Hebrews 4:15) — and He is also the one before whom an apostle drops as if dead. Both. Always both.

**The keys are not in the empire's hand**

Here is why this matters to a prisoner on a rock. Christ tells John the one thing a suffering church most needs and least believes. "I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades" (Revelation 1:18). Rome held the keys to John's cell. Rome did not hold the keys to John's grave. The empire could end his life and could not touch his death, because the door that the empire most relied on — the threat of the tomb — was already unlocked from the inside by a man who walked out of His own.

This is where the curtain pulls back on us. We are not on Patmos. We are comfortable, and our comfort has made the threat of death feel theoretical, which means the comfort of these keys feels theoretical too. So we fear smaller things. The lost job. The damaged reputation. The disapproval of people who will be dead in fifty years. We have outsourced our fear to a hundred little caesars because we no longer believe the one who holds the keys is standing in the room. And He is. He is the head of the body, the church, the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18), and the lampstands among which He walks are not in heaven. They are the churches. He is here, examining, holding, speaking from behind you so that you have to turn.

Look again at how Christ describes Himself to the churches, because it sets the whole book in motion. He is the first and the last, the living one, the one who was dead. The order is the gospel in miniature — first and last, then dead, then living forever. The eternal one entered our death and came out the far side of it still holding the title, and the keys He now carries are keys He took from inside the tomb. No one hands you the keys to a prison He has not been in. Christ holds the keys of death because He has been through that door Himself and returned.

And this is why John must write what he sees and send it to the seven churches. The vision is not a private comfort. It is a letter to congregations under pressure, and the first thing they need to know is not when the end comes. It is who is standing among their lampstands right now. A church that knows the living Christ walks in its midst can lose its building, its standing, even its life, and not lose its center.

Turn around. The voice is not the future calling. It is the living Christ, in the room, with the keys.

He holds death's keys.

## What the Lord Knows About His Church
*Christ examines four churches with eyes like fire and demands not success but repentance*

**Text:** Revelation 2 · **Supporting:** Revelation 1:14 · Jeremiah 2:13 · 1 Corinthians 13:2 · Matthew 7:21-23

Every church keeps a story about itself. The story is almost always kinder than the truth. We grade ourselves on attendance and budget and the warmth of the lobby, and we file the report under *thriving*, and then we go home. Revelation 2 is what happens when the one with eyes like a flame of fire (Revelation 1:14) reads the report Himself.

Four times He begins the same way. "I know your works." Not *I have heard*. Not *it appears*. I know. The risen Christ does not assess His church from the outside, from membership numbers and online metrics. He stands among the lampstands and reads what is actually there.

**He knows what you have left, even when no one notices**

To Ephesus He gives a commendation most of our churches would die for. They worked hard. They endured. They tested false apostles and found them liars. They could not bear evil people. By every metric we use, Ephesus was sound. And then the eyes of fire find the one thing the metrics missed. "But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first" (Revelation 2:4).

Not heresy. Not scandal. They kept the doctrine and lost the affection underneath it, and Christ counts that as a fall — "remember therefore from where you have fallen" (Revelation 2:5). Paul had said the same in another city: if I have all knowledge and have not love, I am nothing (1 Corinthians 13:2). A church can be right about everything and be a clanging gong. I have stood in pulpits defending truths I had stopped loving, and there is no colder place in ministry than being correct and dead at the same time.

**He knows what it costs you, even when the world calls you poor**

Then Smyrna. The shortest letter, and the only church besides Philadelphia that receives no rebuke at all. Christ has nothing against the church that is being crushed. "I know your tribulation and your poverty (but you are rich)" (Revelation 2:9). The parenthesis is the whole gospel. The world's ledger has Smyrna in the red, and heaven's ledger has them wealthy, and the two ledgers will never agree.

He does not promise to spare them. He tells them it is about to get worse — prison is coming, and for some, death. And to that church He says, "Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life" (Revelation 2:10). Not faithful until it gets hard. Faithful unto death. The reward is not escape from the cost. The reward is on the other side of it.

**He knows the compromise you have learned to call tolerance**

Pergamum and Thyatira are harder, because their sin is ours. Pergamum held fast to His name even where Satan's throne was — and tolerated those who taught the people to eat what was sacrificed to idols. Thyatira had love and faith and service and patient endurance, growing works, and tolerated a false prophet who taught God's servants to commit immorality. The pattern is exact. Strong churches with a tumor they had agreed not to remove.

Notice what Christ refuses to do. He will not let the strengths buy off the sin. He commends the love and then names the compromise in the same breath, because faithfulness in nine rooms does not sanctify the tenth. We do the opposite. We tally the good and let it cover the rot, and we call that grace, when it is only cowardice wearing grace's clothes.

**The forsaken fountain, and the one knocking from outside**

We should sit with how exposed these churches were. They did not get to grade their own assignment. The one with eyes of fire walked in unannounced and read what was actually there, and four times He began the same way, *I know* — not your reputation, not your self-report, your works. We organize whole ministries around managing perception, around the story we tell about ourselves to donors and members and ourselves. Christ does not read the brochure. He reads the room, and He reads the heart underneath it, and there is no version of the report we can prepare that He has not already seen to the bottom of.

And notice the strange mercy in the threat to Ephesus. "If not, I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place" (Revelation 2:5). He does not threaten to destroy them. He threatens to leave — to take His presence away and let the church go on existing as a building without a Christ in it, which is the most terrifying judgment of all, because the church would likely never notice He had gone. The lights stay on. The programs run. And the lampstand is dark.

Underneath all four letters runs an ancient diagnosis. Centuries before Patmos, God indicted His people through Jeremiah: "they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water" (Jeremiah 2:13). That is every one of these churches. Ephesus traded the fountain for orthodoxy. Pergamum and Thyatira traded it for accommodation. Two sins — abandoning the living water and digging cracked tanks — and we did the second because we stopped drinking from the first.

What He demands is one word, and it is the hardest word for a successful church to hear. "Repent." Not improve. Not strategize. Repent — turn back to the love you left, the fountain you forsook. Because the alternative is the most frightening sentence in the Gospels, spoken by this same Lord: on that day many will say *Lord, Lord, did we not do many mighty works in your name*, and He will declare, *I never knew you* (Matthew 7:21-23). The terror of Revelation 2 is not that Christ does not know His church. It is that He does — and to those still reading their own kinder report, the door is closing, and His patience is not infinite.

He knows your works.

## The Door He Stands Behind
*To Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea Christ exposes the church that mistakes itself for alive*

**Text:** Revelation 3 · **Supporting:** Matthew 23:27 · Revelation 3:8 · Hosea 12:8 · John 10:9

The most dangerous condition a church can be in is not persecution. It is the gap between its reputation and its reality. Sardis had a name. Laodicea had a balance sheet. Both were corpses that had not yet been told. Revelation 3 is Christ measuring the distance between what a church believes about itself and what He sees, and the distance is fatal.

**The church that has a name and is dead**

"I know your works. You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead" (Revelation 3:1). Sardis had standing. Other churches spoke well of it. And the one with eyes of fire pronounces it a tomb with a good address. This is the exact judgment Jesus laid on the religious leaders of His own day — "you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people's bones" (Matthew 23:27). A name for life and the smell of death underneath. The terrifying thing about Sardis is that it did not know. You can run programs and fill seats over a grave for years before anyone checks the pulse.

His command to Sardis is not *try harder*. It is *wake up*. "Strengthen what remains and is about to die" (Revelation 3:2). Even in the tomb there are embers. The mercy is that He bothers to tell a dead church it is dead, because the diagnosis is itself an act of love. He could have walked past the lampstand. He stopped.

**The church with little power and an open door**

Then Philadelphia, and the tone changes entirely. Of this church Christ has nothing to rebuke — only this: "I know that you have but little power, and yet you have kept my word and have not denied my name" (Revelation 3:8). Little power. That is the church Christ commends without reservation. Not the one with influence and a platform and the ear of the powerful. The one with almost nothing, that held the word and would not deny the name when denying would have been easier.

And to that small, faithful, unimpressive church He makes the promise the powerful never get. "Behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one is able to shut" (Revelation 3:8). The door does not open because the church is strong. It opens because Christ holds the key, the key of David, and what He opens no one shuts. We spend our energy trying to manufacture our own open doors — the right connections, the right strategy, the right cultural moment. Christ gives the open door to the church that had no power to force one and simply kept His word.

And to Philadelphia He gives the promise that frightened first-century believers most needed: an hour of trial is coming on the whole world, and "I will keep you" (Revelation 3:10). Not *I will spare you the trial* — He keeps them through it, the way He kept the witnesses, the way He keeps every church that holds His word with little power. Faithfulness that holds no influence at all is not invisible to Christ for a moment. It is the thing He commends without a single word of rebuke.

**The church that thought itself rich**

Laodicea is the one we cannot escape, because Laodicea is us. "For you say, I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing, not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked" (Revelation 3:17). Seven words of self-assessment, seven words of reality, and not one of them overlaps. The same self-deception haunted Ephraim centuries before: "I am rich, I have found wealth for myself" (Hosea 12:8). Wealth has always been able to talk a soul out of its own poverty.

Lukewarm is the word, and we have softened it into mediocrity, a little less zealous than we should be. That is not what it meant. Laodicea sat near hot springs that cooled and cold streams that warmed, and what reached the city was tepid and nauseating — water you spit out. Christ would rather we were cold than this. Cold knows it needs heat. This church needed nothing, and a church that needs nothing has no use for a Savior, which is why the Savior is on the outside.

**The knock from outside His own church**

So we arrive at the most quoted and least understood verse in the book. "Behold, I stand at the door and knock" (Revelation 3:20). We have turned it into an evangelistic appeal to the unbeliever's heart. Read it where it stands. Christ is knocking on the door of His own church — outside Laodicea, locked out by a congregation so full of itself it never noticed He had stepped into the street. The Lord who walks among the lampstands has been put out of one of them, and He has not kicked the door down. He knocks.

That is the mercy and the indictment at once. He could pronounce the verdict and go. Instead He stands in the cold and offers gold refined by fire, white garments, salve for blind eyes — everything the rich church thinks it already owns. "I am the door," He had said years before. "If anyone enters by me, he will be saved" (John 10:9). The door of the sheep now stands at the door of the church, knocking, because the only way back in is to open to the one we shut out while congratulating ourselves on our wealth.

I do not preach this from above it. I have built ministry on the Laodicean lie, mistaken full rooms for life and a healthy budget for the favor of God, and not noticed the knocking for years at a time. The question Revelation 3 leaves is not whether your church has a name. It is whether the Christ whose name you carry is inside the building — or in the street, still knocking, waiting for someone to hear.

He stands outside, knocking.

## The Only One Worthy
*Behind the chaos of history is an occupied throne, and only the slain Lamb can open the scroll*

**Text:** Revelation 4-5 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 6:1-3 · Daniel 7:9-10 · Philippians 2:8-11 · 1 Peter 1:18-19

When the world feels out of control, the question underneath every other question is whether anyone is on the throne. Not whether God exists in some general sense — whether He is reigning now, over this, over the news that just broke and the diagnosis that just came. Revelation 4 answers before it argues. A door stands open in heaven, and the first thing John sees through it is a throne, and the throne is occupied.

**The throne was never empty**

"Behold, a throne stood in heaven, with one seated on the throne" (Revelation 4:2). John does not describe the face. He describes light — jasper, carnelian, a rainbow like an emerald — and the same thunder and worship Isaiah heard when he saw the Lord high and lifted up and the seraphim crying *Holy, holy, holy* (Isaiah 6:3). Around the throne, twenty-four elders and four living creatures, and they never stop saying it. This is the room behind the curtain. While the empire on earth believes it governs, heaven's worship does not pause to acknowledge Rome at all.

That is the pastoral force of chapter 4. The first reader was a persecuted believer who could see only Caesar's throne — the one with soldiers and taxes and the power to exile a man to a rock. Revelation pulls back the curtain and shows him the throne the soldiers cannot see, already occupied, surrounded by ceaseless worship, the Ancient of Days seated as Daniel saw Him with thrones placed and the court in session and the books opened (Daniel 7:9-10). History is not chaos seeking a ruler. It is a kingdom whose King is seated.

**The scroll no one could open**

Then chapter 5 turns the comfort into a crisis. In the right hand of the one on the throne is a scroll, sealed with seven seals — the whole purpose of God for history, His verdict on the world, His plan to set things right. And a mighty angel asks the only question that matters: "Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?" (Revelation 5:2).

Silence. "No one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll" (Revelation 5:3). And John, the apostle, the one who saw the risen Christ, does something we rarely let ourselves do. He breaks down. "I began to weep loudly because no one was found worthy" (Revelation 5:4). Read that as the human condition. If no one can open the scroll, then God's purposes stay sealed, history has no resolution, the suffering has no meaning, and the persecuted church on Patmos dies for nothing. John weeps because a sealed scroll is a world without redemption.

**The Lion who is a Lamb**

Then the turn that the whole book hangs on. An elder tells John to stop weeping: "the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll" (Revelation 5:5). John hears *Lion*. He turns to see the conqueror. And what he sees is not a lion. "I saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain" (Revelation 5:6).

This is the hinge of Revelation, perhaps of the whole Bible. John is told *Lion* and shown *Lamb*. He is promised a conqueror and given a slaughtered victim, still bearing the marks of its death, standing alive. The conquest of God does not look like the conquest of the empire. Heaven's Lion conquered by being killed. The throne of the universe is won at a cross. The world's whole theory of power — the strong devour the weak, the victor is the one left standing over the body — is overturned in a single image: the slain one stands, and He is the one who reigns.

And why is He worthy? The song says it plainly. "Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation" (Revelation 5:9). Not worthy because He is powerful in the abstract. Worthy because He was slain, and the slaying purchased a people. Peter said the same: you were ransomed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish (1 Peter 1:18-19). The only one in the universe found worthy to govern history is the one who let history kill Him to save us.

**The worship that answers the weeping**

So the room that was silent erupts. The four living creatures, the elders, then myriads of myriads of angels, then every creature in heaven and earth and under the earth and in the sea — the whole created order finds one voice: "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing" (Revelation 5:12). Paul saw this end coming — every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, because He humbled Himself to death on a cross (Philippians 2:8-11). Heaven's worship is not aimed at raw power. It is aimed at sacrificial love that turned out to be the most powerful thing there is.

Here is where it lands on us. We are still tempted to weep over a world that looks sealed. We still suspect that the strong run history and the gentle get crushed. We still reach for the lion's methods — force, the threat, the upper hand — because the Lamb's way looks like losing. And then John turns and the conqueror is a slaughtered Lamb, alive, holding the scroll, and the whole universe falls down. If the throne belongs to the one who was slain, then the way of the Lamb is not the way that loses. It is the only way that finally wins.

This is why the worship of heaven is not sentimental. It is a verdict on the nature of power itself. The universe was not made to reward the predator. It was made to crown the Lamb.

Stop weeping. The scroll is in the right hands.

The Lamb alone is worthy.

## Who Can Stand
*As the Lamb opens the seals and judgment rides, the answer is the multitude washed in His blood*

**Text:** Revelation 6-7 · **Supporting:** Revelation 6:16-17 · Joel 2:11 · Revelation 7:14 · Romans 5:9

The Lamb who was found worthy now opens what He alone could open, and the comfort of chapter 5 becomes the terror of chapter 6. The same hand that was nailed to the cross breaks the seals, and as each one opens, history convulses. Conquest, war, famine, death — the four horsemen — and then the cry of the martyrs under the altar asking how long, and then the sky itself rolled back like a scroll. This is the part of Revelation we would rather skip, and we cannot, because it asks the one question every honest person eventually asks.

**The question the powerful ask when power runs out**

When the sixth seal opens and the heavens shake, watch who panics. "The kings of the earth and the great ones and the generals and the rich and the powerful, and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains" (Revelation 6:15). The whole pyramid of human power — from the emperor down to the slave he owns — runs for the same hole in the ground. And out of that hole comes a prayer, the most honest prayer the godless ever pray: they call to the mountains to fall on them and hide them "from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb" (Revelation 6:16).

The wrath of the Lamb. Hold those two words together, because everything in us wants to separate them. We like the Lamb gentle and the wrath safely abstract. Revelation will not allow it. The same slain Lamb who ransomed a people is the one whose face the rebellious cannot bear. Then comes the question that hangs over the whole book. "For the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?" (Revelation 6:17). Joel had asked it centuries earlier — "the day of the LORD is great and very awesome; who can endure it?" (Joel 2:11). It is not a rhetorical flourish. It is the real question. When the curtain is gone and the throne is unhidden, who is left standing?

**The silence before the answer**

Chapter 7 makes us wait. Four angels hold back the four winds so that the earth is not yet struck, and another angel rises with the seal of the living God, and the judgment pauses — long enough to mark a people. "Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads" (Revelation 7:3). Before the full weight falls, God identifies His own. The pause is mercy with a purpose. The world facing wrath is not abandoned; in the middle of it, God is sealing a people who belong to Him, and the seal is on the forehead, the visible place, the place that says *owned*.

I want us to feel how this would have landed on a church being hunted. To them it would have seemed that Rome held the power to mark people — to brand, to register, to decide who could buy and sell and live. Revelation says there is a prior seal, set by God Himself, that Rome cannot see and cannot break. You are marked before the empire ever gets its hands on you.

**The countless multitude, and how they got there**

Then the answer to *who can stand* walks onto the page, and it is not a handful of the impressive. "After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes" (Revelation 7:9). Standing. The very thing the question asked. The kings hid in caves and could not stand; this uncountable crowd stands in the open before the throne, and they are not the strong of the earth. They are the redeemed of every nation, the people Rome thought it had crushed, on their feet in the one place that matters.

How? John does not know, and an elder tells him. "These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb" (Revelation 7:14). There it is, and it is gloriously offensive to every instinct we have. Their robes are white because they were washed in blood. Not white because they were strong enough to keep them clean. Not white because they earned it under pressure. White because the slain Lamb's blood made them so. Paul said it without the imagery: since we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God (Romans 5:9). The blood that the kings of the earth fled is the blood that washes a people clean and stands them upright.

**Where this leaves us**

The honest answer to *who can stand* is no one — no one on their own merit, not the emperor, not the general, not the religious man counting his works. The day of wrath finds every self-made righteousness hiding in a cave. And then a multitude no one could number stands in the open, not because they were better, but because they were washed.

This is where it stops being about *them* and becomes about you. You will face that throne. The only question worth your anxiety is not whether the day comes but which group you stand in when it does — the great ones begging the mountains to bury them, or the washed multitude on their feet. And the difference between the two is not strength, or résumé, or how well you held up under tribulation. It is blood. His blood, on you, marking you as His before the storm ever reaches your door.

The washed multitude does not stand because the storm was mild. They come out of the great tribulation, not around it. The blood does not exempt you from the cost. It carries you through it and stands you upright on the other side.


The Lamb's people will stand.

## The Prayers That Move Heaven
*The trumpets warn, the church bears witness, and the kingdom of the world becomes the Lord's*

**Text:** Revelation 8-11 · **Supporting:** Revelation 8:3-5 · Exodus 9:23-25 · Revelation 11:3 · Revelation 11:15

We pray as if our prayers evaporate. We say the words, and nothing visibly moves, and over time a quiet unbelief settles in — that prayer is a discipline for our own sakes, a way to feel better, with no real traffic between the closet and the throne. Revelation 8 is the answer to that unbelief, and the answer is staggering. Before a single trumpet of judgment sounds, heaven goes silent, and the reason for the silence is the prayers of ordinary saints.

**The prayers that come up before God**

"And another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne, and the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God" (Revelation 8:3-4). The prayers of all the saints. Not the prayers of apostles and martyrs only — all of them, the ordinary ones, the ones who prayed *how long* in the dark and assumed no one heard. They rose. They reached the throne. They were kept, gathered, held in a golden bowl until the moment came.

And then watch what the angel does with them. "Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, and there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake" (Revelation 8:5). The prayers go up — and the fire comes down. The trumpets of judgment that follow are, in some real sense, the answer to the prayers of the persecuted church. The God who seemed silent was collecting every cry, and at His hour He hurls them back to earth as fire. Heaven does not lose a single prayer of a single saint.

**Judgment that still leaves the door open**

The trumpets sound, and the judgments come in the language of Egypt — hail and fire mixed with blood, as on the day the LORD sent thunder and hail and fire ran down to the earth and struck the land of Egypt (Exodus 9:23-25). The reader is meant to hear the exodus underneath. These are plagues against a new Pharaoh, a new empire that enslaves the people of God. But notice the restraint built into them. A third of this, a third of that — not yet the whole. The trumpets are partial on purpose. They are warnings, not the end. Even here, in the middle of judgment, God is leaving room.

That is the hard mercy of the trumpets, and the text says it plainly and sadly. After the plagues, "the rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands" (Revelation 9:20). The warnings were real warnings. The door was genuinely open. And they would not turn. We do not like a God who judges; we like even less the truth this verse names — that judgment held back to give time for repentance is met by people who use the time to harden. The trumpets are not God's failure to warn. They are humanity's refusal to listen.

**The church that prophesies and dies and rises**

In the middle of all this stands the strangest and most important picture for us — the two witnesses. "And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth" (Revelation 11:3). The number, the sackcloth, the fire from their mouths — the details are debated, but the function is not. The two witnesses are the church, bearing testimony in a hostile world during the whole age between the cross and the end. The church's job, while judgment falls and the world refuses to repent, is to witness. To keep telling the truth in sackcloth.

And the church's witness gets it killed. The beast makes war on the witnesses and conquers them and kills them, and the world throws a party over their corpses, gives gifts, celebrates that the troublesome voice is finally silenced (Revelation 11:7-10). This is the part we must not flinch from. Faithful witness, in this age, often looks exactly like defeat. The bodies in the street. The world celebrating. And then — "after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet" (Revelation 11:11). The pattern of the Lamb, again. Killed, then standing. The church follows its Head down into death and up out of it.

**The seventh trumpet, and the announcement that ends the suspense**

Then the seventh trumpet, and heaven stops warning and starts declaring. Loud voices in heaven announce the thing the whole book has been moving toward: "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever" (Revelation 11:15). Not *will become* in some far-off way the persecuted can only hope for. The announcement is made as accomplished. The verdict of history is read out in heaven before it is visible on earth.

Here is where it presses on us. We pray, and nothing seems to move, and we conclude that the world belongs to the people who hold the levers — the empires, the markets, the ones who decide who can buy and sell. Revelation says no. The kingdom of the world is on its way to becoming the kingdom of our Lord, the verdict is already read in heaven, and the prayers you thought evaporated are in a golden bowl, rising, kept, about to come down as fire. I confess I have prayed like a man who does not believe this, gone through the words while assuming the levers of history were in other hands. They are not. The hand on the censer is the Lamb's, and not one of your prayers has been lost.

The announcement is read in heaven before it is seen on earth, and that gap — between the verdict already given and the world that still looks like the dragon's — is exactly where the church lives, and prays, and waits.


The kingdom belongs to Him.

## The Dragon and the Slain Lamb's People
*The ancient conflict unveiled — and saints who conquer by the blood of the Lamb*

**Text:** Revelation 12-13 · **Supporting:** Genesis 3:15 · Revelation 12:11 · Revelation 13:16-17 · John 16:33

Every age believes its conflict is new. The latest crisis, the latest enemy, the latest threat to the church that no generation has faced quite like this. Revelation 12 pulls the curtain back on all of it and shows the conflict beneath the conflicts — older than Rome, older than any empire, going back to a garden and a promise. What looks like current events is an ancient war, and you are standing in the middle of it.

**The war behind the wars**

John sees a woman about to give birth and a great red dragon waiting "to devour her child the moment it was born" (Revelation 12:4). The child is the Messiah; the dragon is "that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan" (Revelation 12:9). *Ancient.* The word reaches all the way back to Eden, to the first promise of the gospel, when God told the serpent that the woman's offspring would bruise his head and he would bruise its heel (Genesis 3:15). The dragon has been trying to devour the child ever since — through Pharaoh's slaughter of the infants, through Herod's, through every attempt to kill the promised seed before He could crush the serpent's head.

And the dragon failed. The child was caught up to God and to His throne. The cross, which looked like the serpent finally sinking his teeth in, was the heel-bruise that crushed the head. So the dragon, defeated at the cross, does the only thing a defeated enemy can do. He turns on the people of the child. "The dragon became furious with the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring, on those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus" (Revelation 12:17). That is the church. The war you are in is not new. It is the rage of an enemy who already lost the decisive battle and now spends his fury on the Lamb's people, because he cannot reach the Lamb.

**How the dragon now fights**

Chapter 13 shows the dragon's strategy, and it is not horns and fire. It is a beast that rises from the sea — political power, the empire, the state that demands worship — and a second beast from the land that makes the world worship the first. For John's readers the beast wore the face of Rome. In every age it wears a new face, but the move is the same: a power that claims what belongs only to God, and a religious apparatus that blesses the claim and makes resistance look like treason.

And then the detail that has frightened readers for two thousand years. The second beast "causes all, both small and great, both rich and poor, both free and slave, to be marked on the right hand or the forehead, so that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark" (Revelation 13:16-17). We have turned that into a puzzle about microchips and barcodes and missed what it meant to the church first reading it. The mark is the counterfeit of the seal of God from chapter 7. God marks His own on the forehead; the beast marks its own on hand and forehead. Two peoples, two marks, two owners. And the beast's mark controls the economy — you cannot buy or sell, you cannot make a living, unless you belong to the system and worship what it tells you to worship. The dragon's deadliest weapon is not violence. It is the slow pressure to go along, to make the small compromise that keeps you able to buy and sell, until you have worshiped the beast without ever deciding to.

**How the saints win**

So how does a people with no army, no economic power, no way to fight the beast on the beast's terms, actually overcome? Heaven answers in one of the most important verses in the book. "And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death" (Revelation 12:11).

Sit in that sentence, because it overturns everything the dragon counts on. The saints conquer — but not by seizing the beast's power, not by out-fighting it, not by gaining control of the system that marks and sells. They conquer by three things the world counts as weakness. The blood of the Lamb — a victory already won at a cross, applied to them, washing them as in chapter 7. The word of their testimony — they keep telling the truth, like the two witnesses, even when it gets them killed. And they loved not their lives even unto death — the one weapon the dragon cannot answer. The empire rules by the fear of death; it has no hold over people who have stopped fearing it. A church willing to die has already escaped the beast's only real grip.

**Where this finds us**

I will not pretend this is comfortable, and I will not pretend I am above it. The dragon's pressure on me has rarely come as persecution. It has come as the small accommodation that keeps me able to buy and sell — the truth softened so the platform survives, the prophetic word trimmed so the funding holds, the worship of the beast performed in increments I told myself were prudence. That is how the mark goes on. Not in a dramatic moment of denial, but in a thousand quiet trades for the right to keep participating.

And the answer is not a strategy. It is the blood, the testimony, and a love for Christ that outweighs the love of my own life and comfort. The Lamb told His people before any of this, "In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world" (John 16:33). The dragon is real, his war is ancient, his pressure is on your hand and your forehead right now — and he lost at the cross, and the people washed in the Lamb's blood, who will not love their lives more than their Lord, have already won.

They overcame by His blood.

## The Song No One Else Can Learn
*Against the mark of the beast stand the redeemed who bear the Lamb's name and sing a new song*

**Text:** Revelation 14 · **Supporting:** Revelation 14:1 · Revelation 14:3 · Psalm 96:1 · Revelation 14:13

After the dragon and the two beasts, after the mark that controls who can buy and sell, the camera cuts away from the beast — and the first thing we see is not an army. It is a choir. "Then I looked, and behold, on Mount Zion stood the Lamb, and with him 144,000 who had his name and his Father's name written on their foreheads" (Revelation 14:1). Two chapters of the beast's pressure, and the answer to all of it is a people on a mountain, marked with a name, singing.

**Two marks, two peoples, two mountains**

The contrast is deliberate and total. The beast marked its people on the forehead so they could buy and sell. Here stand a people marked on the forehead with the name of the Lamb and the Father. The world had only two options all along — the mark of the beast or the seal of God, the name of the system or the name of the Lamb. There is no unmarked middle ground, no neutral citizen of the empire who belongs to no one. Everyone bears a name on the forehead. The only question is whose.

And the beast's people are gathered on the beast's terms, in the beast's economy. The Lamb's people are gathered on Mount Zion, the mountain of God. The same scene, two mountains, and the church that looked crushed in chapter 13 is standing whole on chapter 14's mountain with its God. The persecution did not reduce their number. There they are, complete, sealed, on their feet beside the Lamb.

**The song you have to be redeemed to learn**

Then John hears them. "And they were singing a new song before the throne... and no one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth" (Revelation 14:3). A new song — the song the psalms kept calling for, "Oh sing to the LORD a new song" (Psalm 96:1) — but with a restriction. No one else could learn it. Not the powerful, not the educated, not the religious who never bowed to the Lamb. The song can only be sung by the redeemed.

There is something here the modern church needs badly. We have assumed the things of God are available to anyone who wants to study them — that worship is a skill, that the new song can be learned by anyone willing to put in the hours. Revelation says no. The new song of the redeemed is not a technique. It is a testimony. You cannot learn it from the outside, because its lyrics are *you were slain and by your blood you ransomed me*, and only the ransomed can sing that truthfully. The world can imitate worship. It cannot sing the song of the Lamb, because it has not been bought.

**The harvest with two outcomes**

Then the chapter turns sober, because a song of the redeemed implies a harvest, and a harvest implies a division. John sees one like a son of man on a cloud with a sharp sickle, and an angel cries, "Put in your sickle and reap, for the hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe" (Revelation 14:15). Two harvests follow — the grain and the grapes, and the grape harvest is thrown into the great winepress of the wrath of God. The same field, gathered two ways. The Lamb gathers His own into the barn; the unrepentant are gathered for judgment.

We would prefer a Christianity that is all barn and no winepress, all gathering and no wrath. Revelation 14 will not give it. The same hour that reaps the redeemed into worship reaps the rebellious into judgment, because a love that finally rescues the oppressed must finally deal with the oppressor. The wrath is not the failure of God's love for His people. It is the other side of it. You cannot rescue the woman from the dragon and leave the dragon untouched.

**Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord**

In the middle of the harvest comes a sentence aimed straight at a church being killed. "And I heard a voice from heaven saying, Write this: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on. Blessed indeed, says the Spirit, that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them" (Revelation 14:13). To a people facing the beast's sword, heaven calls the dead *blessed*. Not pitied. Not defeated. Blessed — at rest, their labor over, their deeds following them into the barn.

This is where it lands on us, and it lands hard precisely because most of us are not being killed. We are being courted. The beast's pressure on a comfortable church is not the sword; it is the offer — sing our song, take our mark, buy and sell on our terms, and you can keep your life and your platform and your peace. And the test of who you belong to is brutally simple. Whose song can you sing? When the worship of the redeemed begins — *worthy is the Lamb who was slain* — is that your native tongue, the song of a people who know they were bought, or is it a tune you perform without ever having paid for the right to mean it?

I have performed it. I have led the song of the Lamb from a stage on days my heart was singing the beast's song under my breath, trading truth for buying-and-selling power and calling it stewardship. The new song cannot be faked forever. It can only be sung by the ransomed, and you sing it best from Mount Zion, marked with His name, on the far side of a cross that bought you.

The song is not a performance you master. It is a confession you have lived. You sing *worthy is the Lamb who was slain* in tune only when the slaying was for you, and you know it.


The Lamb gathers His own.

## The Fall of the City That Could Not Last
*The bowls finish God's wrath, and Babylon — the empire of blood and luxury — falls in one hour*

**Text:** Revelation 15-18 · **Supporting:** Revelation 18:7 · Jeremiah 51:7-8 · Revelation 18:11 · Revelation 18:4

Every empire sells the same lie, and it is the oldest lie there is: *this will last.* Rome believed it. Babylon believed it before Rome. The empire always presents itself as permanent — too big to fall, too rich to fail, the natural and final order of things — and the church, living inside it, half-believes the advertisement. Revelation 15 through 18 is God's reply to the lie of permanence, and the reply is a city that promised forever and fell in an hour.

**The wrath that is finally finished**

The bowls of chapter 16 are the last plagues, "for with them the wrath of God is finished" (Revelation 15:1). The trumpets were partial — a third, a third, warnings with room left for repentance. The bowls are total and final. The time for warning is over. And still, even as they fall, the text records the same refusal we saw with the trumpets: they cursed God and "did not repent and give him glory" (Revelation 16:9). The hardness goes all the way down. A heart set against God does not soften under judgment; it only curses louder. This is the sober truth Revelation keeps forcing on us — that judgment alone has never made a single person repent. Only mercy does that, and the time for mercy is not infinite.

**The city named Babylon**

Then the great vision: a woman, a city, "Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes and of earth's abominations" (Revelation 17:5), drunk on the blood of the saints. *Babylon* is code, and John's readers knew it — the great seductive empire of every age, Rome in their day, the city built on conquest and luxury and self-worship that demands the world bow to it. She sits on the beast. She rides the political power. She is the culture of the empire, its commerce and its idolatry and its appetite, draped in purple and scarlet and gold.

And hear her boast, because it is the boast of every empire and, if we are honest, the quiet boast of every comfortable heart inside one. "In her heart she says, I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see" (Revelation 18:7). I will never grieve. I will never be brought low. I am permanent. Jeremiah had heard the same golden cup centuries before, when the first Babylon fell: "Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD's hand, making all the earth drunken... Suddenly Babylon has fallen and been broken" (Jeremiah 51:7-8). The wine of empire makes the whole world drunk on the dream of permanence, and then, suddenly, the cup shatters.

**The hour, and the merchants who weep for themselves**

The fall, when it comes, comes fast. "In a single hour your judgment has come" (Revelation 18:10). One hour. The city that promised forever is gone in less time than it takes to grieve it. And watch who mourns, because the mourners expose what Babylon really was. The kings weep. The merchants weep. The shipmasters weep. And listen to why the merchants weep: "the merchants of the earth weep and mourn for her, since no one buys their cargo anymore" (Revelation 18:11). They do not grieve the city. They grieve their sales. Babylon's fall is mourned by no one who loved her, only by everyone who profited from her. The whole relationship was a transaction, and when the buying and selling stopped, so did the love.

Then comes the cargo list, and it is a list of luxury — gold, silver, jewels, fine linen, silk, spices, wine, oil — until the very last item, almost thrown in at the end, exposes the whole economy. The cargo includes "slaves, that is, human souls" (Revelation 18:13). There it is. Babylon's commerce, for all its purple and gold, finally trafficked in human beings. The empire that called itself civilization ran on the buying and selling of souls. That is what God brings down in an hour — not just a city, but an entire economy that had learned to price the image of God and sell it.

**Come out of her, my people**

And right in the middle of this, before the city falls, comes a command aimed not at Babylon but at the church inside her. "Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues" (Revelation 18:4). My people. There are believers inside Babylon — there always are — and the danger to them is not that the empire will persecute them, though it might. The danger is that they will be so at home in her luxury and her commerce that they share her sins and go down with her. The call is not to flee the world geographically. It is to stop belonging to the empire's heart, to stop drinking the wine of permanence, to live as people who know the city is falling even while they walk its streets.

This is the verse that finds me, because I am not a persecuted believer in a hostile empire. I am a comfortable one, deeply at home in a Babylon I have learned to call normal life — its commerce, its appetites, its quiet confidence that things will go on as they are. *Come out of her* is not a word I find easy, because coming out costs the comfort I have arranged my life around. The empire does not have to imprison the church. It only has to make the church comfortable enough that *come out of her* sounds like fanaticism.

The lie is *this will last.* The truth is that everything built on blood and luxury and self-worship is already condemned, already an hour from falling, and the only thing that survives the hour is the people who heard *come out* and obeyed. Where is your ultimate home — in the city that promised forever, or with the Lamb who outlasts it? If that question makes you uneasy, that unease is mercy, and the door is still open.

Babylon falls in an hour.

## The Rider on the White Horse
*Heaven erupts in worship, and the Faithful and True rides out with the sword of His word*

**Text:** Revelation 19 · **Supporting:** Revelation 19:6-7 · Isaiah 11:4 · Revelation 19:13 · Revelation 19:15

Babylon has fallen, and the question that follows any fall is *now what.* When the empire that promised forever collapses in an hour, when the city built on blood is gone, what fills the silence? Revelation 19 answers with two things in sequence, and the order matters. First a wedding. Then a war. Heaven does not respond to Babylon's fall with grim relief. It responds with worship and a marriage, and only then does the Rider come out.

**The Hallelujah that follows the fall**

Four times in the opening verses of chapter 19 heaven cries one word — *Hallelujah* — the only place in the entire New Testament where it appears. And what triggers it is not a pleasant thing to modern ears. Heaven shouts hallelujah because Babylon has fallen and "he has avenged on her the blood of his servants" (Revelation 19:2). We have trained ourselves to find judgment embarrassing, something to apologize for. Heaven finds it worthy of worship, because the saints whose blood Babylon drank now see their God set the account right. A God who never judged the empire that trafficked in souls would not be loving. He would be indifferent. The hallelujah is the sound of love that finally acts.

Then the worship turns from the fall to the wedding. "Hallelujah. For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready" (Revelation 19:6-7). This is the destination the whole book has been driving toward — not merely the destruction of the false city, but the marriage of the Lamb to His people. The opposite of Babylon the prostitute is the Bride. The empire offered a transaction; the Lamb offers a marriage. And the Bride is granted to clothe herself in fine linen, bright and pure, which is the righteous deeds of the saints — given to her, granted, not earned, the white robes of chapter 7 now become a wedding dress.

**The Rider, and what He is called**

Only after the wedding does heaven open and the Rider come. "Then I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse. The one sitting on it is called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and makes war" (Revelation 19:11). This is the return of Christ, and Revelation paints Him with deliberate care, because everything in us wants to either tame this scene or revel in it for the wrong reasons. He has eyes like fire. On His head are many crowns. He is the King who was the Lamb.

And His name — "he is clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and the name by which he is called is The Word of God" (Revelation 19:13). Note carefully whose blood is on the robe before the battle has even begun. The robe is dipped in blood when He rides out, before a single enemy has fallen. It is His own blood. The conqueror returns wearing the marks of the cross. The Lamb who was slain is the Rider who reigns. He does not arrive having forgotten Calvary. He arrives still wearing it.

**The sword is His mouth**

Then the detail that disarms every fantasy of a violent, swaggering Christ. How does the Rider make war? "From his mouth comes a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations" (Revelation 19:15). Not in His hand — from His mouth. His weapon is His word. This is Isaiah's promised King, who "shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked" (Isaiah 11:4). The long reign of deception — the dragon's lies, the beast's propaganda, the prostitute's seduction — does not end through negotiation, and it does not end through the kind of violence the empire understands. It ends with a word. The same word that spoke creation into being speaks the lie into nothing.

This is everything. The world's powers conquer with swords in their hands and bodies on the ground. Christ conquers with a sword from His mouth and His own blood on His robe. He does not become the beast in order to defeat the beast. He defeats it as the Lamb, with the truth, having already bled. There is no negotiation with the lie at the end — no summit, no compromise, no peace treaty between the truth and the empire of deception. The Word of God simply speaks, and the long lie is over.

**Where this leaves the church that waits**

I have to be honest about how this exposes me, because I have wanted the wrong Christ to come back. In my worst moments I have wanted a Rider who fights the way the world fights, who comes back to win the culture war on the empire's terms, with the empire's weapons, leaving my enemies on the ground and my tribe on top. That is not the Rider Revelation shows. The Rider's robe is dipped in His own blood. His sword is His word. He has crowns precisely because He was crucified. A church longing for a conquering Christ who has forgotten the cross is longing for the beast and calling it Jesus.

And the call to that church is not to take up the empire's sword in the meantime. It is to be the Bride who has made herself ready, clothed in the righteousness granted to her, waiting for the wedding, bearing witness with the only weapon her Lord uses — the word of her testimony — until the heavens open and the Faithful and True comes out. The empires fall in an hour. The marriage of the Lamb lasts forever. And the one who ends the long reign of the lie does it the same way He always has: as the slain Lamb, speaking the truth, His own blood on His robe.

Faithful and True rides out.

## The Books and the Throne
*The dragon's defeat is sealed, the dead stand before the throne, and the only refuge is the Lamb's book*

**Text:** Revelation 20 · **Supporting:** Revelation 20:11-12 · Daniel 7:10 · Revelation 20:15 · Revelation 21:27

There is one appointment no one breaks, no empire postpones, no amount of money reschedules. We organize whole lives around avoiding the thought of it. Revelation 20 will not let it stay avoided. After the dragon is finally thrown into the lake of fire, after his long war on the saints is ended, John sees the scene that the entire human race is moving toward whether it believes in it or not — a throne, and the dead standing before it, and books being opened.

**The throne nothing can flee**

"Then I saw a great white throne and him who was seated on it. From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them" (Revelation 20:11). Earth and sky themselves flee — and find no place to hide. If the creation cannot escape this throne, no creature will. We spend our lives finding places to hide from God — in work, in pleasure, in religion, in busyness, in the comfortable assumption that the reckoning is for other people. Revelation 20 names the end of every hiding place. At the great white throne there is no cave, no distraction, no platform, no curated self. Just the dead, standing, in the open, before the throne.

"And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened" (Revelation 20:12). *Great and small.* The categories that ran the whole world — power and weakness, wealth and poverty, the celebrated and the forgotten — dissolve at this throne. The emperor and the slave he owned stand in the same line. Daniel saw this court convene long before John did: "the court sat in judgment, and the books were opened" (Daniel 7:10). Every life is recorded. Nothing is lost, nothing is hidden, nothing is forgotten by the God who keeps the books.

**The two sets of books**

And there are two kinds of books, and the difference between them is the difference between everything. "And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done" (Revelation 20:12). The first set records deeds — what each person actually did, the complete and accurate account of a life. If that were the only book, the scene would be hopeless, because no life survives an honest reading of its own record. The books of deeds condemn every one of us, great and small, without exception. A perfect account of what I have done is a guilty verdict, and I know it, and so do you.

But there is another book, mentioned almost in passing and carrying the whole weight of human destiny. "And another book was opened, which is the book of life" (Revelation 20:12). Two kinds of books at the throne — the books of what you did, and the book of whose you are. And the final verse of the chapter makes the stakes unmistakable. "And if anyone's name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire" (Revelation 20:15).

Read that with care, because it cuts against everything we assume. The deciding factor at the throne is not whether your deeds were good enough — they were not, mine were not, no one's were. The deciding factor is whether your name is written in the book of life. Deliverance is not earned in the books of deeds. It is granted in the book of life. And whose book is it? Revelation will tell us a chapter later — it is "the Lamb's book of life" (Revelation 21:27). The book that saves belongs to the one who was slain. Your name is written there in His blood or it is not written there at all.

**The honesty the throne demands**

I cannot preach this from a safe distance, and I will not try. I have spent stretches of my life living as a practical atheist about this throne — preaching it on Sunday and forgetting it by Tuesday, ordering my days as though the books would never be opened and my name's place in the Lamb's book were a settled thing I never had to think about again. The great white throne strips that comfort away. It asks the one question that matters more than every other question I have ever asked from a pulpit: is my name written in the Lamb's book of life? Not, was I a good pastor. Not, did I build something. Is my name in the book that belongs to the slain Lamb.

And here is the mercy hidden inside the terror, the reason this chapter is gospel and not just dread. The book of life exists. There is a book whose entries are not deeds but names, written by the Lamb, secured by His blood and not by your performance. The throne that no one can flee is also the throne where the slain Lamb has already secured a people. The God who keeps a perfect record of your deeds keeps a second book, and in it He writes the names of those He has bought, and what He has written cannot be unwritten.

The throne is coming. The books will open. The only question that will matter when earth and sky have fled and no place is found is whether the one who keeps the books has written your name in the book that belongs to the Lamb. If that question unsettles you tonight, do not run from the unease. Run to the Lamb whose book is still open and whose blood still writes names.

Do not soften the lake of fire into a metaphor for self-exclusion, and do not let it become a club you swing at people you dislike. It is the just end of a life that kept perfect time in the books of deeds and never had its name written in the book of the Lamb. The terror and the mercy stand in the same chapter, and only one of the two books can save you.


Be written in His book.

## All Things New
*The end is not escape from earth but God coming down to dwell, where every tear is wiped away*

**Text:** Revelation 21-22 · **Supporting:** Revelation 21:3-4 · Genesis 2:10 · Revelation 22:3 · Revelation 22:20

We have gotten the end of the story wrong, and the error is not small. We have made the Christian hope a story about leaving — souls escaping a doomed earth, flying off to a disembodied heaven somewhere else, the material world finally discarded as the thing we were trying to get away from all along. That is not how Revelation ends. The last vision is not the church going up. It is God coming down. The direction of the entire Christian hope is downward — heaven descending to earth, the King moving in, God making His home with us.

**God comes down**

"And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God" (Revelation 21:2). Coming down. Then the loud voice from the throne announces what the whole book — what the whole Bible — has been driving toward: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God" (Revelation 21:3). This is the thread that runs from Eden through the tabernacle through the temple through the incarnation, finally and forever fulfilled. God walked with man in a garden and man hid. God dwelt with Israel in a tent and a temple behind a veil. God became flesh and dwelt among us and we crucified Him. And here, at the end, the dwelling is permanent, unveiled, unbroken. He will dwell with them. The whole story of the Bible is God's relentless determination to live with His people, and at the end He gets His way.

**The tears, and the hand that wipes them**

Then the promise that has carried more grieving believers through more graveside services than perhaps any other in Scripture. "He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away" (Revelation 21:4).

Notice how personal it is. He does not announce that tears will cease in some general administrative way. He wipes them away — God Himself, with His own hand, from your own eyes, one face at a time. This is not a cosmic policy. It is a Father bending down to a child. And notice what is named as gone: death, mourning, crying, pain. Every enemy that the dragon ever used against the people of God — every weapon Babylon and the beast ever wielded, finally and including the last one, death — is not managed or reduced. It is gone. The former things have passed away.

**The garden restored, and the curse undone**

What John sees inside the city pulls the whole Bible into a circle. "Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb" (Revelation 22:1), and on either side the tree of life. A river and the tree of life. These were the furniture of Eden — "a river flowed out of Eden to water the garden" (Genesis 2:10), and the tree of life stood in its midst, the tree we were exiled from when the curse fell. The story that began in a garden we were driven out of ends in a garden-city we are welcomed into, and the tree we lost is given back.

And then the verse that undoes the oldest wound in the world. "No longer will there be anything accursed" (Revelation 22:3). The curse — pronounced in Genesis 3, the thorns and the sweat and the pain and the exile and the death, the shadow over every human life since the garden — is lifted. Not endured forever. Not merely survived. Removed. The slain Lamb who took the curse on a tree gives back the tree of life, and the long ache of a cursed world is finally, fully over.

**Behold, I make all things new**

And in the middle of it all, the one on the throne speaks — one of the very few times in the book He speaks directly — and says the sentence the entire creation has been groaning to hear. "Behold, I am making all things new" (Revelation 21:5). Not all new things. All things new. He does not throw the creation away and start over with something else. He takes this world, this scarred and cursed and grieving world, the very world the dragon thought he had ruined, and He makes it new. The marriage, the garden, the dwelling, the wiped-away tears — this is what the Lamb purchased with His blood. He did not bleed to evacuate a few souls from a doomed planet. He bled to make all things new.

This is where the whole series has been going, and where it leaves us. I confess I have lived as though the end of the story were escape — as though faith were a strategy for getting out, for enduring this world until I could leave it. Revelation corrects me at the last. The hope is not that I get out. The hope is that God gets in — that He comes down, moves in, wipes the tears with His own hand, undoes the curse, and makes everything, including me, new. That hope is meant to change how I live now, in a world still groaning, still under the dragon's fading war: I am not waiting to escape it. I am waiting for its King to come and renew it, and I am to live now as a citizen of the city that is coming down.

The book ends not with a timeline but with a longing, and the longing is mutual. The Lamb says, "Surely I am coming soon," and the church, the Bride, can only answer, "Amen. Come, Lord Jesus" (Revelation 22:20). The last word does not belong to the dragon, or the beast, or Babylon, or death. It belongs to the slain and reigning Lamb, who holds the keys, who opened the scroll, who rode out faithful and true, and who is even now coming down to make His home with us and wipe away every tear.

Behold, He makes everything new.
